title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 31
paragraphs: The valet came back to the cottage and told the count that Moscow was burning. The count put on his dressing gown and went out to look. Sonya and Madame Schoss, who had not yet undressed, went out with him. Only Natasha and the countess stayed in the room. Petya was no longer with the family. He had gone on with his regiment, which was heading for Troitsa.

When the countess heard that Moscow was on fire, she began to cry. Natasha, pale and fixed in her gaze, sat on the bench under the icons, exactly where she had sat down on arrival, and paid no attention to her father's words. She was listening to the adjutant's ceaseless moaning three houses away.

"Oh, how terrible," said Sonya, coming back from the yard chilled and frightened. "I think the whole of Moscow will burn. There's an awful glow! Natasha, do look! You can see it from the window," she said to her cousin, evidently wanting to distract her.

But Natasha looked at her as if she did not understand, and fixed her eyes again on the corner of the stove. She had been in this stupor since morning, when Sonya had decided, for some unaccountable reason, to tell Natasha about Prince Andrew's wound and about his being with their party. This had surprised and annoyed the countess. She had seldom been as angry with anyone as she was with Sonya. Sonya had cried and begged to be forgiven, and now, as if trying to make up for her fault, she gave her cousin constant attention.
"Look, Natasha, how dreadfully it's burning!" she said.
"What's burning?" asked Natasha. "Oh, yes, Moscow."

As if she wanted not to offend Sonya and to be rid of her, she turned her face to the window and looked out. It was obvious that she could not see anything. Then she settled back into her former posture.
"But you didn't see it!"
"Yes, really I did," Natasha replied, in a voice that begged to be left in peace.
The countess and Sonya both understood that, naturally, neither Moscow nor the burning of Moscow nor anything else could seem important to Natasha.

The count came back and lay down behind the partition. The countess went over to her daughter and touched her head with the back of her hand, as she used to when Natasha was ill. Then she touched her forehead with her lips, as if to feel whether she had a fever, and finally kissed her.
"You're cold. You're trembling all over. You'd better lie down," said the countess.
"Lie down? All right, I will. I'll lie down at once," said Natasha.

That morning, when Natasha was told that Prince Andrew was seriously wounded and traveling with their party, she had at first asked many questions. Where was he going? How was he wounded? Was it serious? Could she see him? But then they told her that she could not see him, and that he was seriously wounded but his life was not in danger. After that she stopped asking questions and stopped speaking altogether. Evidently she did not believe what they told her, and was convinced that whatever she said, she would be told the same thing. All the way she had sat motionless in a corner of the coach with wide open eyes, with that look the countess knew so well and feared so much. Now she sat in the same way on the bench where she had placed herself on arriving. She was planning something, and was either deciding it or had already decided it in her mind. The countess knew this, but what it might be she did not know, and that alarmed and tormented her.
"Natasha, undress, darling. Lie down on my bed."
Only the countess had a proper bed, made up on a bedstead. Madame Schoss and the two girls were to sleep on hay on the floor.

"No, Mamma, I'll lie down here on the floor," Natasha replied irritably. She went to the window and opened it. Through the open window the adjutant's moans came more distinctly. She put her head out into the damp night air, and the countess saw her slim neck shaking with sobs and throbbing against the window frame. Natasha knew it was not Prince Andrew who was moaning. She knew he was in the same yard as they were, in a part of the hut across the passage. But this dreadful, incessant moaning made her sob. The countess exchanged a look with Sonya.
"Lie down, darling, lie down, my pet," said the countess, softly touching Natasha's shoulders. "Come, lie down."
"Oh, yes... I'll lie down at once," said Natasha, and she began undressing in a hurry, tugging at the tapes of her petticoat.

She threw off her dress and put on a dressing jacket. Then she sat down on the bed that had been made up on the floor, with one foot tucked under her. She jerked her thin, rather short plait to the front and began replaiting it. Her long, thin, practiced fingers quickly unplaited it, replaited it and tied it up. Her head moved from side to side out of habit, but her eyes, feverishly wide, stared straight ahead. When she had finished getting ready for the night, she sank gently onto the sheet spread over the hay, on the side nearest the door.
"Natasha, you'd better lie in the middle," said Sonya.
"I'll stay here," muttered Natasha. "Do lie down," she added crossly, and buried her face in the pillow.

The countess, Madame Schoss and Sonya undressed hastily and lay down. The small lamp in front of the icons was the only light left in the room. But in the yard there was light from the fire at Little Mytishchi, a mile and a half away. Through the night came the noise of people shouting in a tavern that Mamonov's Cossacks had set up across the street, and the adjutant's unceasing moans could still be heard.

For a long time Natasha lay listening closely to the sounds reaching her from inside and outside the room, and did not move. First she heard her mother praying and sighing and her bed creaking under her. Then came Madame Schoss's familiar whistling snore and Sonya's gentle breathing. Then the countess called to Natasha. Natasha did not answer.
"I think she's asleep, Mamma," said Sonya softly.
After a short silence the countess spoke again, but this time no one replied.
Soon afterward Natasha heard her mother's even breathing. Natasha did not move, though her little bare foot, sticking out from under the quilt, was growing cold on the bare floor.

A cricket chirped in a crack in the wall, as if celebrating a victory over everybody. A cock crowed far off, and another answered nearby. The shouting in the tavern had died down. Only the adjutant's moaning could be heard. Natasha sat up.
"Sonya, are you asleep? Mamma?" she whispered.

No one replied. Natasha got up slowly and carefully, crossed herself, and stepped warily onto the cold, dirty floor with her slim, supple, bare feet. The floorboards creaked. Placing each foot with care, she ran like a kitten the few steps to the door and took hold of the cold door handle.
It seemed to her that something heavy was beating rhythmically against all the walls of the room. It was her own heart, sinking with alarm and terror and overflowing with love.

She opened the door, stepped over the threshold and onto the cold, damp earthen floor of the passage. The chill refreshed her. With her bare feet she touched a sleeping man, stepped over him, and opened the door into the part of the hut where Prince Andrew lay. It was dark inside. In the farthest corner, on a bench beside a bed with something lying on it, stood a tallow candle with a long, thick, smoldering wick.

From the moment she had been told that morning about Prince Andrew's wound and his being there, Natasha had been determined to see him. She did not know why she had to. She knew the meeting would be painful, but that only made her more certain it was necessary.

All day she had lived only in the hope of seeing him that night. Now that the moment had come, she was filled with dread of what she might see. How was he maimed? What was left of him? Was he like that incessant moaning of the adjutant's? Yes, he was exactly like that. In her imagination he was that terrible moaning in person. When she saw an indistinct shape in the corner and mistook his knees, raised under the quilt, for his shoulders, she imagined a horrible body lying there, and stood still in terror. But an irresistible impulse drew her forward. She cautiously took one step and then another, and found herself in the middle of a small room full of baggage. Another man, Timokhin, was lying in a corner on the benches beneath the icons, and two more, the doctor and a valet, lay on the floor.

The valet sat up and whispered something. Timokhin, kept awake by the pain in his wounded leg, gazed with wide-open eyes at this strange apparition of a girl in a white chemise, dressing jacket and nightcap. The valet's sleepy, frightened cry, "What do you want? What's the matter?" made Natasha hurry toward what lay in the corner. That body looked horribly unlike a man, but she had to see him. She passed the valet, the snuff fell from the candle wick, and she saw Prince Andrew clearly, with his arms outside the quilt, just as she had always seen him.

He was the same as ever. But the feverish color of his face, his glittering eyes turned rapturously toward her, and above all his neck, delicate as a child's, bared by the turned-down collar of his shirt, gave him a peculiarly innocent, childlike look, such as she had never seen on him before. She went up to him and dropped to her knees in a swift, supple, youthful movement.
He smiled and held out his hand to her.
